trouble.p: No DNA / very faint band on the gel

cf.c: Too little starting material, or tissue not ground finely
cf.f: Use 100 mg fresh tissue ground to a fine powder; coarse grinding leaves cells intact.
Extend 65 °C incubation to 60 min with inversion every 10 min; pre-warm CTAB buffer before adding.
Decant against the light and watch the pellet; leave 20–30 μL rather than draining fully.

cf.c: Isopropanol step too short or too warm
cf.f: Precipitate at −20 °C for at least 30 min (overnight is better); use chilled isopropanol.

cf.c: Pellet over-dried and will not redissolve
cf.f: Air-dry only until translucent, never to a white crust; redissolve at 55–60 °C for 15 min in TE.

trouble.tip: Always run 3–5 μL on a 0.8% gel before proceeding — finding out at the PCR stage wastes a day.

trouble.p: DNA is sheared (smear instead of a tight high-molecular-weight band)

cf.f: Mix by gentle inversion only, from lysis onwards.
Use cut or wide-bore tips for viscous lysates.
Grind under liquid nitrogen without letting the powder thaw; extract immediately.
Keep lysis to 45–60 min.

trouble.tip: A smear still works for PCR but is unusable for RFLP, long amplicons or genome work.

trouble.p: Brown or coloured pellet / DNA not clean (A₂₆₀/A₂₈₀ off)

cf.c: Polyphenols and pigments co-precipitated (common in okra, cotton, mango tissue)
cf.f: Add 1–2% PVP to the CTAB buffer and 0.2% β-mercaptoethanol fresh before use.

cf.c: Polysaccharide contamination (ratio ~1.6 or lower, viscous pellet)
cf.f: Raise NaCl in the buffer to 1.4–2 M; repeat the chloroform:isoamyl step twice.
Repeat chloroform extraction; ensure clean phase separation without carrying the interface.

cf.c: RNA contamination (ratio > 2.0, smear at the gel front)
cf.f: Treat with RNase A (10 μg/mL, 37 °C, 30 min) and re-precipitate.

trouble.tip: Record A₂₆₀/A₂₈₀ (target 1.8–2.0) and A₂₆₀/A₂₃₀ (target > 2.0) for every extraction in the log.

trouble.p: DNA will not dissolve, or degrades in storage

cf.f: Warm at 55–60 °C in TE for 15–30 min; leave overnight at 4 °C rather than pipetting hard.

cf.c: Stored in water instead of TE
cf.f: Store in TE — the EDTA chelates Mg²⁺ and blocks nucleases; water at slightly acidic pH slowly hydrolyses DNA.
Aliquot into working tubes; keep the master stock at −20 °C (−80 °C for long term) and thaw once.

cf.c: Nuclease contamination from gloves or bench
cf.f: Change gloves, use fresh filter tips, keep a dedicated clean area.

trouble.tip: Label every tube with sample code, concentration and date — unlabelled DNA becomes useless DNA.

trouble.p: No amplification (blank lanes, ladder fine)

cf.c: Template too concentrated or containing inhibitors
cf.f: Dilute template 1:10 and 1:100 and retry — inhibitor dilution often rescues the reaction.
Repeat with a fresh master mix; making mix for n+10% and dispensing before template reduces pipetting errors.
Drop annealing by 3–5 °C, or run a gradient if the thermal cycler allows.
Use a fresh aliquot; store working primers at −20 °C in small aliquots.

cf.c: Taq lost activity (left out of the freezer)
cf.f: Use a fresh tube of enzyme; always keep Taq in a cold block while setting up.

trouble.tip: Include a known positive control in every run — without it you cannot tell a failed reaction from a true negative.

trouble.p: Non-specific bands / smeary product

cf.f: Raise annealing by 2–5 °C.

cf.c: Too much template or too many cycles
cf.f: Reduce template and cut cycles to 30–32.
Lower Mg²⁺ stepwise (1.5 → 1.0 mM) — high Mg²⁺ stabilises mismatched priming.
Set up on ice and use a hot-start polymerase where available.

trouble.tip: Optimise one variable at a time and record the winning condition against that primer pair.

trouble.p: Band in the no-template control (contamination)

cf.f: Discard all reagent aliquots, decontaminate pipettes and racks, use fresh water and primers.

cf.c: Post-PCR work done in the setup area
cf.f: Keep pre- and post-PCR pipettes, tips and benches strictly separate; never open product tubes in the setup area.
Use filter tips for every PCR step.

trouble.tip: Once contamination sets in, replacing reagents is faster than chasing it — start with fresh water and primer aliquots.

trouble.p: Primer-dimer (bright band below ~100 bp)

cf.f: Reduce primers to 0.2–0.4 μM.

cf.c: Little or no template competing for primers
cf.f: Confirm template quality; dimers dominate when the target is absent.

cf.c: Reactions held at room temperature before cycling
cf.f: Assemble on ice; start cycling promptly.

trouble.tip: Dimers waste reagents and confuse quantification — they matter far more in qPCR than in routine PCR.

trouble.p: No bands visible, though the run looked normal

cf.c: Stain omitted, or added to agarose above 60 °C
cf.f: Add stain after cooling to ~55 °C; alternatively post-stain the gel for 20 min.
Stop when the tracking dye reaches two-thirds; smaller fragments migrate faster than the dye.

cf.c: Polarity reversed — DNA migrated out of the wells
cf.f: Wells at the cathode (black); DNA runs towards the anode (red).

cf.c: Loading dye omitted so sample floated away
cf.f: Always mix sample with loading dye before loading.

trouble.tip: If in doubt, load a ladder in the first and last lanes — it reveals polarity and running problems immediately.

trouble.p: Bands are smiling, distorted or fuzzy

cf.f: Run at 5 V/cm or lower; long runs are better done slowly.
Replace running buffer; do not reuse indefinitely.

cf.c: Buffer strength mismatched between gel and tank
cf.f: Cast and run in the same buffer at the same strength.

cf.c: Gel set unevenly or comb removed carelessly
cf.f: Cast on a level surface and lift the comb straight up under buffer.

trouble.tip: TAE gives better resolution for large fragments; TBE runs cooler for long high-voltage runs.

trouble.p: Wells tore or samples leaked between lanes

cf.c: Comb removed before the gel set fully
cf.f: Allow at least 30 min setting; remove the comb after submerging in buffer.

cf.c: Agarose percentage too low for handling
cf.f: Use ≥ 0.8% for routine work.
Keep sample volume within well capacity; dilute if necessary.

trouble.tip: Load slowly with the tip just above the well — pushing the tip in punctures the base.

trouble.p: Poor standard curve efficiency (outside 90–110%)

cf.c: Pipetting errors in the dilution series
cf.f: Prepare fresh 10-fold dilutions, vortexing at each step; use a calibrated micropipette.

cf.c: Inhibitors in the template concentrating at low dilutions
cf.f: Test a wider dilution range; the linear portion reveals the usable range.
Redesign primers for 80–150 bp amplicons with Tm 58–62 °C.

trouble.tip: An efficiency of 90–110% (slope ≈ −3.3, R² > 0.99) is the acceptance criterion — record it with every assay.

trouble.p: Multiple melt-curve peaks or high NTC signal

cf.f: Lower primer concentration; redesign if persistent.
Raise annealing temperature; verify a single band on a gel.
Prepare fresh mix with new water and primer aliquots.

trouble.tip: Always run the melt curve — SYBR reports any double-stranded DNA, not just your target.

trouble.p: High variation between replicates

cf.f: Spin the plate briefly before loading.

cf.c: Uneven sealing or a scratched optical film
cf.f: Seal firmly across all wells; never touch or write on the optical surface.

cf.c: Reaction volumes too small to pipette reliably
cf.f: Keep reactions ≥ 10 μL; make a mix rather than pipetting components per well.

trouble.tip: Replicate Cq values should agree within 0.5 cycles.

trouble.p: Bacterial contamination overrunning the plates

cf.f: Increase hypochlorite contact to 2 min (or HgCl₂ 30 s), then rinse in three water changes.
Add streptomycin (30–100 mg/L) after autoclaving, once cooled to ~45 °C — it is heat-labile.

cf.c: Plates opened outside the laminar flow
cf.f: All transfers in the cabinet, blower running 10–15 min beforehand.

cf.c: Medium poured too thin or plates not dried
cf.f: Pour ~20 mL per plate and dry lids ajar in the cabinet for 15 min before use.

trouble.tip: Streptomycin added to hot medium is destroyed — the commonest cause of 'the antibiotic isn't working'.

trouble.p: Fast-growing contaminants (Rhizopus, Aspergillus, Penicillium) swamp the target

cf.c: Ambient spore load in the lab
cf.f: Clean the cabinet, check the pre-filter, avoid opening sporulating cultures nearby.
Use half-strength PDA or a selective medium (rose bengal for soil fungi, Nash-Snyder for Fusarium).
25 ± 2 °C in the BOD incubator; higher temperatures favour weeds.
Use 3–5 mm pieces from the lesion margin, not from decayed centres.

trouble.tip: Rose bengal restricts colony spread — useful when one fast fungus keeps covering the plate.

trouble.p: Culture will not sporulate

cf.f: Transfer to a poor medium: half-strength PDA, oat meal agar, water agar with sterile host tissue.
Incubate under 12 h near-UV/day light alternation.
Revive from a stock slant or re-isolate from an infected host.

cf.c: Species simply sporulates poorly in vitro
cf.f: Use the hyphal-tip method rather than single spore isolation.

trouble.tip: Passing the culture through the host plant restores both sporulation and virulence.

trouble.p: Medium did not set, or is too soft / too hard

cf.f: Standard is 15–20 g/L; check the calculation with the Formulations tab.

cf.c: Acidic medium hydrolysed the agar during autoclaving
cf.f: Adjust pH after autoclaving where the protocol demands acidity, or add acid to cooled medium.
Do not exceed 121 °C for 15–20 min for media.

cf.c: Old agar stock or repeated remelting
cf.f: Avoid remelting a batch more than twice.

trouble.tip: Media that repeatedly fail to set are usually being autoclaved too long or at too low a pH.

trouble.p: Cultures dry out or die in storage

cf.f: Seal caps with parafilm; store at 4 °C.
Cover the slant to 1 cm above the agar tip with twice-autoclaved liquid paraffin.
Subculture routine slants every 3–6 months and maintain the register.

cf.c: Refrigerator running too cold / freezing the slants
cf.f: Confirm 4 °C, not below — freezing kills many mycelia.

trouble.tip: Keep two independent copies of every important isolate, ideally in two locations.

trouble.p: No growth from a diseased sample

cf.c: Sample taken from an old or dead lesion
cf.f: Sample the advancing margin of a fresh lesion; dead tissue holds only saprophytes.
Bacteria are surface-shallow — 30–60 s hypochlorite is usually enough, or rinse only.
Cut tissue into sterile water and wait 10–20 min for streaming; then streak.

cf.c: Plant treated with bactericide/antibiotic before sampling
cf.f: Collect from untreated plants where possible.
Hold plates 5–7 days before discarding as negative.

trouble.tip: The ooze test in a drop of water under the microscope confirms bacterial involvement before you isolate.

trouble.p: Mixed growth / no single colonies

cf.f: Flame the loop between each of the four quadrants and cool it before touching the agar.
Dilute the suspension before streaking (serial dilution figure in the protocols).
Dry plates in the cabinet for 15 min before streaking so the surface absorbs the streak.
Add cycloheximide or use a selective medium.

trouble.tip: A well-streaked plate is worth two re-isolations — slow down at the quadrant streaking step.

trouble.p: Gram staining gives inconsistent results

cf.f: Use an 18–24 h culture; older cells lose the ability to retain crystal violet and read as Gram-negative.
Make a thin, even smear and heat-fix gently — thick smears retain stain regardless of wall type.
Decolourise for a few seconds only, until the run-off just clears.
Pass the slide through the flame 2–3 times; do not roast it.

trouble.tip: Run a known Gram-positive and Gram-negative control alongside whenever results look doubtful.

trouble.p: Stain too dark or structures obscured

cf.c: Too much mycelium in the mount
cf.f: Tease out a small tuft only; spread it thinly in the stain.
One small drop is enough; blot the edge with tissue if needed.
Warm the slide gently over a flame (do not boil) to clear the mount.

trouble.tip: Take the mount from the colony margin — the centre is dense and often sterile.

trouble.p: Air bubbles under the coverslip

cf.f: Lower it at a 45° angle from one edge, letting the liquid spread ahead of it.
Use enough that it just fills the coverslip area.
Tap the coverslip gently with a needle tip.

trouble.tip: Blot excess fluid from the edge with tissue, not by pressing the coverslip down.

trouble.p: Blurred or dim image

cf.f: Raise the condenser and open the iris until the field is evenly bright.

cf.c: Oil objective used without oil, or oil on a dry objective
cf.f: Use immersion oil only with the 100× objective; clean it off with lens tissue afterwards.
Clean with lens tissue — never with paper tissue or cloth.
Thin the preparation and use a fresh coverslip.

trouble.tip: Set Koehler illumination once at the start of the session and everything after it looks better.

trouble.p: No colour development in positive controls

cf.c: Substrate old or exposed to light
cf.f: Prepare pNPP fresh; keep it dark until use.

cf.c: Sodium azide carried into the conjugate or substrate step
cf.f: Azide inhibits alkaline phosphatase — exclude it from those buffers entirely.
Use the recommended dilution; store conjugate at 4 °C, never frozen.

cf.c: Incubation too short or too cold
cf.f: Follow times at 37 °C; check the incubator temperature.

trouble.tip: Azide contamination is the single commonest cause of a dead ELISA plate.

trouble.p: High background in blanks and healthy controls

cf.f: Wash 3–4 times with PBS-T, soaking briefly each time; empty plates fully between washes.
Block with 2% skim milk or BSA for a full hour at 37 °C.
Titrate the antibody to find the working dilution.

cf.c: Plates allowed to dry between steps
cf.f: Add the next reagent immediately after washing.

trouble.tip: Positive is conventionally > 2× the mean healthy-control absorbance — record the threshold with each plate.

trouble.p: EDTA will not dissolve

cf.f: EDTA disodium salt dissolves only as the pH approaches 8.0 — add NaOH pellets gradually while stirring.

cf.c: Solution not stirred or too cold
cf.f: Stir continuously on the magnetic stirrer; gentle warming helps.
Confirm 93.05 g per 500 mL for 0.5 M using the Formulations tab.

trouble.tip: Adjust the pH first, then make up to the final volume — never the other way round.

trouble.p: pH drifts or the meter reads unstable

cf.f: Calibrate with fresh pH 4.0, 7.0 and 9.2 buffers before critical work.
Store in 3 M KCl, never in distilled water; clean protein/media deposits with the recommended solution.

cf.c: Solution not stirred, or temperature differs from calibration
cf.f: Stir gently and measure at the same temperature as calibration.
Discard standards once opened for a few weeks; never pour used buffer back into the bottle.

trouble.tip: pH set before autoclaving shifts afterwards — check and record the post-autoclave value where it matters.

trouble.p: Buffer or medium precipitates, or grows contamination on storage

cf.c: Phosphate buffers precipitate with calcium/magnesium salts
cf.f: Dissolve and autoclave salt groups separately, then combine when cool.
Follow the storage column in the Chemicals tab; TBE stocks precipitate slowly — discard when crystals appear.
Use freshly autoclaved distilled water and clean bottles.

cf.c: Bottle repeatedly opened at the bench
cf.f: Aliquot working volumes so the stock is opened rarely.

trouble.tip: Label every bottle with contents, concentration, date and preparer — undated buffer is untrustworthy buffer.

trouble.p: Reagents lose activity sooner than expected

cf.c: Enzymes and antibiotics left at room temperature
cf.f: Keep Taq, enzymes and conjugates in a cold block whenever out of the freezer/fridge.
Add antibiotics, vitamins and heat-labile fungicides to cooled (~45 °C) medium after autoclaving.

cf.c: Light-sensitive reagents stored in clear bottles
cf.f: Store rose bengal, catechol, IAA and similar in amber bottles or wrapped in foil.
Aliquot on first use — the second thaw is where most activity is lost.

trouble.tip: The Chemicals tab lists the storage requirement for each item; check it before shelving a new bottle.

trouble.p: Medium is contaminated even though it was autoclaved

cf.c: Load too large or bottles packed tightly, so steam never reached the centre
cf.f: Fill flasks to no more than two-thirds; leave space between them; extend the hold for volumes above 1 L.

cf.c: Air not displaced from the chamber
cf.f: Let the chamber discharge freely until steam runs steadily before closing the valve; trapped air is cooler than steam at the same pressure.

cf.c: Caps screwed tight, preventing steam entry and creating pressure
cf.f: Loosen caps a quarter turn; cover flask mouths with cotton plugs and foil.

cf.c: Timing started before the gauge reached 121 °C / 15 psi
cf.f: Count the 15–20 min hold only from the moment the set temperature is reached.

cf.c: Contamination introduced after autoclaving, while pouring
cf.f: Pour inside the laminar flow, flame the flask mouth, and do not pour below 45 °C in a draught.

trouble.tip: If contamination appears in every batch, test the autoclave with a spore strip or autoclave tape placed at the centre of the load, not on the outside.

trouble.p: Agar does not set, or sets too soft

cf.c: Agar concentration too low, or the medium was over-diluted
cf.f: Use 15–20 g/L agar for plates; check the volume made up after autoclaving, not before.
Do not autoclave longer than 20 min at 121 °C; repeated re-autoclaving weakens the gel.

cf.c: Acidic medium hydrolysed the agar during sterilisation
cf.f: Sterilise the medium at its natural pH and adjust with sterile acid afterwards; do not autoclave below pH 5.

cf.c: Agar not fully melted before dispensing
cf.f: Bring to a rolling boil with stirring until the solution is clear, with no visible flecks.

trouble.p: Heavy condensation on the plate lids

cf.f: Cool the medium to 45–50 °C before pouring; it should feel warm but bearable on the wrist.
Leave plates undisturbed in the flow until set, then stack; store inverted.

cf.c: Plates stored the wrong way up
cf.f: Always store and incubate inverted, so condensation collects on the lid and not the agar.

trouble.tip: Wet agar surfaces let bacteria and fast fungi spread across the whole plate.

trouble.p: Medium darkened, caramelised or smells burnt

cf.c: Sugars overheated, particularly in media with dextrose
cf.f: Reduce hold time; for sugar-rich media autoclave at 115 °C for 20 min instead of 121 °C.

cf.c: Direct heating on a hot plate without stirring
cf.f: Melt with constant stirring, or use a water bath; never let the flask base go dry.
Melt only what is needed; repeated melting darkens the medium and degrades nutrients.

trouble.p: Antibiotic or fungicide in the medium had no effect

cf.c: Added before autoclaving and destroyed by heat
cf.f: Add antibiotics, streptomycin and most fungicides after autoclaving, once the medium is at 45–50 °C.

cf.c: Stock solution old or stored badly
cf.f: Prepare antibiotic stocks fresh, filter-sterilise, store at −20 °C and use within the recommended period.

cf.c: Concentration calculated on the pre-autoclave volume
cf.f: Calculate on the final volume; note evaporation losses in long cycles.
Change to a different agent; for persistent bacteria use two agents, or acidify the medium instead.

trouble.p: pH is wrong after autoclaving

cf.c: pH shifts on heating and on cooling
cf.f: Set pH before autoclaving allowing for a drop of about 0.2 units; always re-check on the cooled medium.

cf.c: Phosphate buffers change pH with temperature
cf.f: Calibrate and measure at the temperature the medium will be used at, and record which.

cf.c: Adjusted with concentrated acid or alkali added too fast
cf.f: Add dropwise with stirring; overshoot then back-titration adds salt and changes the medium.

trouble.p: Mites moving between plates and carrying contamination

cf.c: Mites entering from old stock cultures or the incubator
cf.f: Discard infested plates by autoclaving, not in the bin; clean the incubator and shelves thoroughly.
Seal with parafilm or cling film; store working cultures in closed boxes.
Stand culture boxes in a tray with a shallow layer of oil or acaricide-treated paper as a barrier.

cf.c: Trails of mixed growth across the agar
cf.f: Recognise the sign early — irregular contaminated tracks are mite trails, not splash contamination.

trouble.tip: Mites can destroy an entire culture collection in weeks. Inspect stocks every fortnight.

trouble.p: Culture is sectoring — a different-looking wedge appears

cf.c: Spontaneous mutation or degeneration on repeated subculture
cf.f: Sub-culture from a hyphal tip within the original sector, not from the new one.
Examine microscopically before assuming degeneration; re-isolate by single spore if in doubt.
Maintain stocks on a lean medium such as water agar or PDA at half strength.

trouble.p: Isolate has lost pathogenicity after repeated subculture

cf.c: Attenuation from long maintenance on artificial medium
cf.f: Restore by passage through the host plant, then re-isolate from the lesion.

cf.c: Too many transfers from the working culture
cf.f: Keep a master stock under mineral oil, in sterile soil or at −80 °C, and work from copies.

cf.c: Selection for fast-growing, less virulent variants
cf.f: Preserve a single-spore culture at the outset and return to it rather than to the working plate.

trouble.tip: Record the passage number of every isolate; pathogenicity data from a high-passage culture is not comparable with early work.

trouble.p: Fungus grows well but will not sporulate

cf.f: Move to a lean medium — water agar with sterile host tissue, oat meal agar, or carnation leaf agar.
Give a 12 h near-UV or daylight cycle; many Alternaria, Fusarium and Colletotrichum species need it.

cf.c: Temperature above the optimum for sporulation
cf.f: Sporulation usually needs a lower temperature than growth; try 20–25 °C.

cf.c: Culture too young or too old
cf.f: Assess after 7–14 days; some species sporulate only after the colony reaches the plate edge.
Scrape the mycelium, or expose to alternating wet and dry cycles.

trouble.p: Bacterial culture turned mucoid, or lost its colony character

cf.f: Maintain on a defined medium and preserve in glycerol at −80 °C.
Streak for single colonies and select one matching the original description.

cf.c: Culture held too long between transfers
cf.f: Transfer every 2–4 weeks for working cultures; do not rely on plates older than a month.

trouble.p: Stored cultures dead when revived

cf.c: Mineral oil layer too thin or the slant dried
cf.f: Cover slants with at least 1 cm of sterile oil above the agar surface.
Use 15–20% glycerol for bacteria; freeze fungal plugs in 10% glycerol; avoid repeated freeze–thaw.
Oomycetes survive poorly on dry storage — keep on hemp seed or in sterile water at 15–18 °C, not frozen.
Revive on a rich medium first, then move to the maintenance medium.

trouble.p: Inoculated plants show no symptoms

cf.c: Inoculum concentration too low or not viable
cf.f: Check viability by plating before inoculating; standardise the spore or cell concentration.

cf.c: Wrong growth stage of the host
cf.f: Inoculate at the stage the disease occurs naturally; seedlings and mature plants often differ.
Provide the temperature and a humid period the pathogen requires; most foliar fungi need 12–48 h of leaf wetness.

cf.c: No wound where the pathogen needs one
cf.f: Wound-inoculate for pathogens that cannot penetrate intact tissue; state clearly in the method which was used.
Include a known susceptible check in every experiment, or a negative result cannot be interpreted.
Use a low-passage or host-passaged culture.

trouble.tip: A pathogenicity test without a susceptible check and a mock-inoculated control cannot prove anything either way.

trouble.p: Control plants developed symptoms too

cf.f: Separate treatments physically; inoculate controls first, and change gloves between treatments.

cf.c: Pathogen already present in the soil, seed or planting material
cf.f: Use sterilised soil and tested seed; check the planting material before starting.

cf.c: Shared irrigation water or a common tray
cf.f: Water at the base individually; do not stand treatments in a shared tray.
Compare with the abiotic possibilities — nutrient deficiency, salt, phytotoxicity — before recording them as infection.

trouble.p: Inoculated plants died quickly of something else

cf.c: Inoculum concentration far above natural levels
cf.f: Reduce to a level comparable with natural inoculum; excessive doses cause toxicity, not disease.

cf.c: Culture filtrate or medium carried over with the inoculum
cf.f: Wash the spore suspension by centrifugation and resuspend in sterile water.

cf.c: Root damage during soil drenching or transplanting
cf.f: Handle roots gently; allow plants to establish before inoculating.
Maintain humidity without saturating the medium.

trouble.p: Disease scores vary widely between replicates

cf.f: Agitate the suspension continuously while inoculating; standardise droplet number and volume per plant.
Randomise the layout and re-randomise periodically; record the position of each pot.

cf.c: Plants differing in age or vigour at inoculation
cf.f: Select uniform plants; discard outliers before, not after, treatment.
Use a defined scale with a picture key, and have the same person score throughout, blind to treatment where possible.

trouble.p: Poisoned food plates show growth even at high concentration

cf.c: Fungicide added to hot medium and degraded
cf.f: Add to the medium at 45–50 °C, after autoclaving, and mix thoroughly before pouring.

cf.c: Fungicide not dissolved, so it settled out
cf.f: Dissolve in the appropriate solvent first; include a solvent-only control.

cf.c: Formulated product used as though it were technical grade
cf.f: Calculate on the active ingredient, not the product weight; state which was used.
Compare with a sensitive reference isolate on the same batch of plates before concluding resistance.

trouble.tip: Include an untreated control on the same batch of medium; comparing across batches introduces more variation than the treatment.

trouble.p: Inhibition percentages are inconsistent between replicates

cf.c: Inoculum discs cut from different parts of the colony
cf.f: Take discs from the actively growing margin of a colony of the same age each time.
Pour a fixed volume per plate; depth changes the effective concentration.
Measure when the control plate reaches the plate edge, and record the day.

cf.c: Diameter measured in one direction only
cf.f: Measure two perpendicular diameters and average them.

trouble.p: Dual culture shows no zone of inhibition

cf.c: Antagonist and pathogen grow at very different rates
cf.f: Give the slower organism a head start of 24–48 h, and state the interval used.
Use a neutral medium; PDA favours many fungi over bacterial antagonists.
Absence of a zone does not mean absence of antagonism — check for mycoparasitism or competition microscopically.
For volatile-mediated antagonism use the sealed inverted-plate method instead.

trouble.p: Chromatogram shows double peaks throughout

cf.c: Culture was not pure — two organisms amplified
cf.f: Re-isolate by single spore or single colony and re-sequence; this is the commonest cause.

cf.c: Multiple ITS copies differing within the isolate
cf.f: Clone the product and sequence several clones, or use a different locus.
Raise the annealing temperature; check the PCR gave a single clean band before sending.

cf.c: Two templates carried over in the reaction
cf.f: Repeat the PCR from a fresh dilution with a clean pipette set.

trouble.tip: Never submit a sequence for identification if the chromatogram is doubled — the consensus will belong to neither organism.

trouble.p: Sequence is short, noisy or fails after a few hundred bases

cf.c: Too little or too much template sent
cf.f: Quantify and dilute to the sequencing facility's stated range; excess template is as bad as too little.

cf.c: Product not cleaned of primers and dNTPs
cf.f: Purify the PCR product by column or gel extraction before submission.
Re-run the PCR to eliminate dimer, then purify.

cf.c: Secondary structure or a poly-A tract
cf.f: Sequence from the opposite primer and assemble both directions.

trouble.p: BLAST match is ambiguous or looks wrong

cf.c: Match is to a poorly identified or mislabelled database entry
cf.f: Prefer sequences from type material or from a recognised culture collection; check who deposited it.

cf.c: ITS cannot separate closely related species in the genus
cf.f: Add a second locus — TEF-1α for Fusarium, β-tubulin for Colletotrichum and Penicillium, LSU for broader placement.

cf.c: Query sequence includes primer or low-quality ends
cf.f: Trim the ends and re-run; a few bad bases at the start shift the match badly.
Look at query coverage and e-value together; a 99% match over 40% coverage means little.
Confirm the molecular result against morphology; disagreement means one of them is wrong.

trouble.tip: A sequence identifies the culture you sequenced, not necessarily the pathogen — it must be tied back to a pathogenicity test.

trouble.p: Saprophytes swamp the blotter plates

cf.f: Surface-sterilise in 1% sodium hypochlorite for 1–2 min and rinse three times in sterile water where the method allows.
Moisten to saturation but pour off free water; standing water spreads bacteria and Rhizopus.
Incubate at 20–25 °C; higher temperatures favour storage fungi over the target.
Space seeds so they do not contact one another — usually 10 per 90 mm plate.

trouble.tip: Deep-freezing the plates for 24 h after the first day checks seed germination and lets the seed-borne fungi grow out.

trouble.p: Poor germination confounds the count

cf.f: Break dormancy by the recommended method for that crop before testing.

cf.c: Hypochlorite too strong or rinsing inadequate
cf.f: Reduce concentration or contact time; rinse thoroughly.
Record the germination percentage separately and report infection on the basis of seeds plated, stating both.

trouble.p: Result does not match the field observation

cf.f: Draw a composite sample by the prescribed method — several probes from different points in the lot.
Use at least 400 seeds for a routine test; smaller samples cannot detect low infection reliably.

cf.c: Method cannot detect the pathogen in question
cf.f: Match the method to the pathogen — blotter for many fungi, agar plate for others, embryo count for loose smut, wash test for spores.

trouble.p: Very few nematodes recovered from the Baermann funnel

cf.c: Water level not touching the sample
cf.f: Ensure the tissue or soil is just submerged; nematodes must be able to swim out and down.
Leave 24–48 h; active migration takes time, and sedentary stages will not move at all.
Process fresh; dried samples give very poor recovery.

cf.c: Too much soil on the sieve, so nematodes could not migrate
cf.f: Use a thin layer — no more than about 1 cm deep.

cf.c: Mesh too fine, or tissue paper blocked
cf.f: Use two layers of facial tissue on a coarse support; a blocked barrier traps everything above it.

trouble.p: Cobb's sieving loses most of the nematodes

cf.c: Sieve series wrong for the target
cf.f: Use a coarse sieve to remove debris, then collect on a 325-mesh (45 μm) sieve for most plant-parasitic genera.

cf.c: Water poured too fast, washing nematodes through
cf.f: Pour gently down the side; allow settling time between decantings.

cf.c: Suspension not allowed to settle before decanting
cf.f: Wait 30–60 s for soil to settle but not the nematodes, then decant promptly.
Repeat the decanting three to five times; single passes recover a fraction.

trouble.p: Root staining shows no giant cells or females

cf.c: Roots too old or too woody
cf.f: Sample young feeder roots 3–5 weeks after inoculation.
Clear in sodium hypochlorite before staining; unstained pigment masks the structures.

cf.c: Stain too weak or destaining overdone
cf.f: Boil in acid fuchsin briefly; destain in acidified glycerol only until the root tissue clears, checking under the microscope.
Look at the galls or swellings themselves, sectioned or squashed, not the root surface.

trouble.p: Sap inoculation gives no infection

cf.f: Extract in cold buffer with a reducing agent; work on ice and inoculate immediately.

cf.c: No abrasive used, or leaves not wounded
cf.f: Dust with carborundum (600 mesh) or celite before rubbing; wounding is essential.

cf.c: Rubbed too hard and the leaf was destroyed
cf.f: Support the leaf from beneath and rub gently in one direction; rinse afterwards with water.
Add 2% PVP or nicotine to the extraction buffer for hosts rich in phenolics.

cf.c: The virus is not mechanically transmissible
cf.f: Many begomoviruses and phloem-limited viruses are not — use grafting or the vector instead.

trouble.tip: Inoculate an assay host known to react, in parallel, so a negative result can be interpreted.

trouble.p: ELISA readings drift or edge wells differ from the centre

cf.c: Uneven incubation temperature across the plate
cf.f: Incubate in a still incubator, not a draught; avoid stacking plates.
Cover the plate; some workers leave the outer ring as buffer-only wells.
Check every well drains; blot firmly between washes.
Read at a fixed time and record it; do not read one plate at 30 min and the next at 90.

trouble.p: Healthy control gives a positive reading

cf.f: Cross-absorb the antiserum with healthy plant extract.
Change tips between samples; do not reuse the trough for different antisera.
Increase blocking time, or the concentration of the blocking agent.

cf.c: Plate contaminated from an earlier step
cf.f: Use a fresh plate; do not re-use plates.

trouble.p: Indicator host shows unexpected or no symptoms

cf.f: Choose the indicator known to respond — Chenopodium for local lesions, Nicotiana glutinosa for TMV, and so on.
Keep indicators at moderate temperature and good light; high temperature suppresses many symptoms.
Symptoms may be from a second virus; confirm by serology or PCR.
Use young plants at the two- to four-leaf stage.

trouble.p: Disease incidence figures are not reproducible between surveyors

cf.c: No agreed definition of an affected unit
cf.f: Define beforehand what counts as diseased — plant, leaf, tiller or fruit — and use it consistently.
Fix the pattern in advance: number of quadrats, spacing, and how the edges are handled.

cf.c: Assessment by eye without a key
cf.f: Use a standard area diagram or a defined severity scale; train together on the same plants first.
Exclude border rows, which are exposed differently to inoculum and to spray drift.

trouble.p: Samples arrive at the laboratory rotten or dried

cf.c: Collected in polythene bags and left in the sun
cf.f: Use paper bags inside a cool box; polythene sweats and rots the tissue within hours.
Process within 24–48 h; refrigerate at 4 °C if it must be held.

cf.c: Whole plants collected when a lesion margin would do
cf.f: Collect the advancing margin of the lesion with healthy tissue attached — that is where the pathogen is alive.
Label with host, variety, location, date, growth stage and symptom description at the moment of collection.

trouble.tip: A specimen without collection details is of limited value however good the diagnosis.

trouble.p: Symptoms do not match any described disease

cf.f: Consider nutrient deficiency, phytotoxicity, salinity, waterlogging, frost and lightning before pursuing a pathogen.
Scattered, patchy spread suggests a biotic cause; uniform patterns along rows or field edges suggest abiotic or management factors.
Mixed causes are common; record everything present rather than fixing on the first explanation.

cf.c: Insect or mite damage mistaken for disease
cf.f: Examine with a hand lens for the pest itself, and check the leaf undersides.

trouble.p: pH meter drifts or will not stabilise

cf.f: Store the bulb in storage solution or 3 M KCl, never in distilled water and never dry.

cf.c: Junction blocked by protein or precipitate
cf.f: Clean by the manufacturer's method; soak in dilute HCl or a cleaning solution and recondition.
Calibrate with fresh buffers, two points bracketing the expected value; discard buffer poured back into the bottle.

cf.c: Temperature difference between buffer and sample
cf.f: Allow both to reach the same temperature, or use automatic temperature compensation.

cf.c: Sample poorly buffered or stirring inconsistently
cf.f: Stir at a constant slow rate and allow the reading to settle before recording.

trouble.p: Balance readings drift or will not settle

cf.c: Balance not level, or the bench vibrating
cf.f: Level using the bubble; place on a solid bench away from centrifuges and foot traffic.

cf.c: Draught from air conditioning or the laminar flow
cf.f: Use the draught shield and close the doors; do not weigh next to a running flow cabinet.
Use glass or metal, or an antistatic device; static is worse in dry weather.
Weigh hygroscopic materials quickly in a closed vessel; tare the closed vessel first.

cf.c: Not warmed up or not calibrated
cf.f: Leave switched on and calibrate at the interval recorded in the log book.

trouble.p: Centrifuge vibrates or the rotor is noisy

cf.f: Balance opposite tubes by weight, not by eye; use a water blank if the number is odd.
Stop immediately and re-seat the rotor; never run a rotor that was not felt to engage.
Check the maximum speed for the rotor and the tube type in use.
Stop and report; do not continue running a machine that has begun to vibrate.

trouble.tip: Stop a vibrating centrifuge at once. A rotor failure at speed is dangerous.

trouble.p: Incubator or BOD is not holding temperature

cf.c: Door opened too often, or overloaded
cf.f: Group the work; leave space for air circulation between plates and shelves.

cf.c: Set point drifted or the controller mis-set
cf.f: Verify against an independent thermometer placed at shelf level, not just the display.

cf.c: Sited in direct sun or beside a heat source
cf.f: Move away from windows, ovens and autoclaves.

cf.c: Vents blocked or the fan failed
cf.f: Check that vents are clear and the fan runs; report a failed fan.

trouble.p: Laminar flow does not maintain sterility

cf.c: Working too close to the front edge
cf.f: Work at least 15 cm inside the cabinet; the front region is not protected.

cf.c: Filter overdue for replacement, or velocity low
cf.f: Check the manometer or velocity reading against the service record; arrange servicing.

cf.c: Cabinet run for too short a time before use
cf.f: Run the blower for 15–20 min before starting work.

cf.c: Movement across the work area, or talking over open plates
cf.f: Move slowly, keep hands downstream of sterile items, and do not pass anything over an open plate.
Keep the working area clear; a crowded cabinet has turbulence, not laminar flow.

trouble.p: Percentage disease data behave badly in analysis

cf.c: Percentages are not normally distributed near 0 or 100
cf.f: Apply an arcsine (angular) transformation for percentage data before analysis, and state that you did.
Use a square-root transformation for count data, or an appropriate generalised model.
Consider a transformation that handles zeros, or a model appropriate to the distribution.

cf.c: Transformation applied but means back-transformed carelessly
cf.f: Analyse on the transformed scale and back-transform means for presentation, reporting the error on the transformed scale.

trouble.tip: State the transformation in the methods. A reviewer will ask, and results are not comparable without it.

trouble.p: Treatment differences look real but are not significant

cf.f: Decide replication in advance from expected variation, not after seeing the data.

cf.c: Variation between replicates larger than between treatments
cf.f: Identify the source — position, plant age, inoculum — and block against it in the design.
Match the analysis to the design; a split-plot analysed as a randomised block gives wrong conclusions.
Several leaves from one plant are not replicates of the treatment; the plant or pot is the unit.

trouble.p: AUDPC values are not comparable between experiments

cf.f: Use the same intervals and total period, or report standardised AUDPC divided by the duration.
State the scale and convert to a common basis before comparing.

cf.c: First assessment made after the epidemic had started
cf.f: Begin assessments before symptoms appear so the early curve is captured.

trouble.p: Pressed specimens turn black or become mouldy

cf.f: Change blotters daily at first; use a plant drier or a warm airy place, not a closed press in a humid room.
Section thick organs before pressing; blot cut surfaces.
Keep with a desiccant and inspect periodically; naphthalene deters insects but does not stop mould.
Allow surface water to evaporate before pressing.

trouble.p: Preserved specimens in fluid have faded or the fluid has clouded

cf.f: Use FAA for structural work; formalin–acetic–alcohol preserves shape but not colour.

cf.c: Colour lost — normal in most fluids
cf.f: Photograph the fresh specimen for the record; do not rely on the jar for colour.

cf.c: Jar not sealed, so the fluid evaporated and concentrated
cf.f: Seal tightly and top up; check stored jars annually.
Fix promptly; delayed fixation allows autolysis and clouding.
